distinctions_drawn: Semantic meaning vs. ontological truth conditions
Said of vs. in a subject
Grammatical, logical, metaphysical, and scientific subjecthood
Immanent form vs. separate Platonic form
explicit_definitions_given: Synonymous predication: same name and same account
Homonymous predication: same name but different account
Primary substance: neither said of a subject nor in a subject
Universal: said of many subjects, dependent on primary substances for concrete realization

dialectical_engagement.objection_handling: Englebretsen's objection is incorporated and qualified rather than dismissed; Gyekye's thesis is retained only in a structural or metaphorical sense.
objections_raised: Semantic incompleteness does not entail ontological dependence
Reducing universals to incomplete symbols undermines definition and universal science
Prohibition of non-substantial subjects cannot ban all universal subjects in discourse

philosophical_orientation.sentiment: Neutral and analytic, aiming at dialectical resolution.
philosophical_orientation.thematic_focus: Ontology, philosophy of language, logic, epistemology of science.

structural_organization.structure_type: Thesis-antithesis-synthesis with progressive refinement; each section repeats and deepens the previous paragraph's content.

summary_of_core_decisions: The text resolves the Gyekye-Englebretsen debate by distinguishing semantic, ontological, and epistemic dependence. Aristotle's universals are not mere incomplete symbols, but they are also not separate substances; they are immanent forms that are ontologically dependent on primary substances yet epistemically prior. The regress of predication is blocked only by understanding the prohibition of non-substantial subjects as a demand for ultimate explanatory grounding, not as a ban on universals as subjects in discourse.
